documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1 — Synthesis involving Carbanions: Chalcone
problems.statement: The aim of this experiment is to condense acetophenone and benzaldehyde in a mixed aldol condensation. After spontaneous dehydratation, an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone is obtained: chalcone, 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-on.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.statement:
### a) Starting the condensation reaction

In a $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ ground-neck Erlenmeyer (conical) flask, dissolve about $5\ \mathrm g$ of potassium hydroxide, $\mathrm{KOH}$ ($50$ pellets), in $30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of water, then add slowly, under stirring, $20\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol. From the automatic dispensers, add $9.6\ \mathrm g$ ($0.08\ \mathrm{mol}=9.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) of acetophenone and $8.5\ \mathrm g$ ($0.08\ \mathrm{mol}=8.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) of benzaldehyde. Set up a condenser in the vertical reflux position and reflux vigorously while stirring the mixture with the magnetic stirrer for an hour.

### b) Isolation of the crude chalcone

After refluxing, cool the contents of the Erlenmeyer flask in an ice bath. The chalcone should crystallize. If crystals do not appear, scratch the inside wall of the flask with a glass rod. Collect the crystals in a Büchner funnel, wash them with a little ice-cold ethanol, then air dry and weigh the crystals.

### c) Recrystallization of the chalcone

Recrystallize this crude chalcone from ethanol, using a $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker. Use the heating plate located in the hood (fume chamber). When crystallization is over (wait long enough and scratch if necessary), collect the crystals in a Büchner funnel and air dry them.

Give your entire product to the supervisor, who will measure its mass and melting point.

Do not breathe the vapour while recrystallizing and measuring the melting point. It contains irrigating chalcone!!!

parts.statement: Write the mechanism for this reaction.
Give the mass of the crystals of the crude chalcon obtained and calculate the yield of crude product.
Calculate the yield of recrystallized product based on starting material and calculate the efficiency of the recrystallization process.

solution.incompleteReason: The warning's “irrigating chalcone!!!” and the request's “crude chalcon” are retained as printed. The obtained collection supplies only the mechanism for 1.1. No actual crude or recrystallized product masses, melting point, yields, recrystallization efficiency or worked results for 1.2–1.3 are supplied.

problems.title: Problem 2 — Qualitative Analysis

sections.title: Equipment
sections.statement:
Five flasks are labelled 2.1 through 2.5. Each contains an aqueous solution of a colourless metal nitrate. Except for silver nitrate, the concentrations of the nitrates used to prepare these solutions are all $0.1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

Also available are pH indicator paper and the following three reagents of a concentration of about $5\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, contained in flasks labelled 2.6 through 2.8:

| Flask | Reagent |
| --- | --- |
| 2.6 | Hydrochloric acid |
| 2.7 | Aqueous ammonia solution |
| 2.8 | Sodium hydroxide solution |

Beware: these solutions are all concentrated and corrosive.

parts.statement: Carry out reactions between each reagent and each solution. For each of solutions 2.1 through 2.5, record your observations for each reaction observed.
Write the name of the cation contained in each of solutions 2.1 through 2.5 in the corresponding space on the answer sheet.
For each cation identified, write the equation for each reaction observed.

sections.statement:
The solutions are aluminium(III) nitrate, calcium(II) nitrate, lead(II) nitrate, silver(I) nitrate and zinc(II) nitrate.

**Aluminium(III) nitrate**

$\mathrm{Al^{3+}+HCl}$: no reaction.

$$\mathrm{Al^{3+}+3NH_3+3H_2O\longrightarrow Al(OH)_3}\downarrow\mathrm{+3NH_4^+}$$

$$\mathrm{Al^{3+}+3OH^-\longrightarrow Al(OH)_3}\downarrow$$

$$\mathrm{Al(OH)_3+OH^-\longrightarrow [Al(OH)_4]^-(aq)}$$

**Calcium(II) nitrate**

$\mathrm{Ca^{2+}+HCl}$: no reaction.

$$\mathrm{Ca^{2+}+2OH^-\longrightarrow Ca(OH)_2}\downarrow$$

**Lead(II) nitrate**

$$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+2Cl^-\longrightarrow PbCl_2}\downarrow\qquad\text{in cold solutions}$$

$$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+2NH_3+2H_2O\longrightarrow Pb(OH)_2}\downarrow\mathrm{+2NH_4^+}$$

$$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+2OH^-\longrightarrow Pb(OH)_2}\downarrow$$

$$\mathrm{Pb(OH)_2+2OH^-\longrightarrow [Pb(OH)_4]^{2-}(aq)}$$

**Silver(I) nitrate**

$$\mathrm{Ag^++Cl^-\longrightarrow AgCl}\downarrow$$

$$\mathrm{Ag^++NH_3+H_2O\longrightarrow AgOH}\downarrow\mathrm{+NH_4^+}\qquad\text{or }\mathrm{Ag_2O}$$

$$\mathrm{AgOH+2NH_3\longrightarrow [Ag(NH_3)_2]^+(aq)+OH^-}$$

$$\mathrm{Ag^++OH^-\longrightarrow AgOH}\downarrow$$

$$\mathrm{2AgOH\longrightarrow Ag_2O+H_2O}$$

**Zinc(II) nitrate**

$\mathrm{Zn^{2+}+HCl}$: no reaction.

$$\mathrm{Zn^{2+}+2NH_3+2H_2O\longrightarrow Zn(OH)_2}\downarrow\mathrm{+2NH_4^+}$$

$$\mathrm{Zn(OH)_2+4NH_3\longrightarrow [Zn(NH_3)_4]^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-}$$

$$\mathrm{Zn^{2+}+2OH^-\longrightarrow Zn(OH)_2}\downarrow$$

$$\mathrm{Zn(OH)_2+2OH^-\longrightarrow [Zn(OH)_4]^-(aq)}$$

The generic reactions have not been turned into invented sample identities.

problems.title: Problem 3 — Titration of Oxygen Dissolved in Water (Winkler's method)
problems.statement: In aqueous alkaline solution, dissolved oxygen oxidizes manganese(II) hydroxide to hydrated manganese(III) oxide, written as $\mathrm{Mn(OH)_3}$ for simplification. In acidic solution, manganese(III) ions oxidize iodide ions to iodine. The iodine formed is titrated with a sodium thiosulphate solution.

sections.title: Data
sections.statement:
| Redox couple | Electrode potential at pH 0 / V | Electrode potential at pH 14 / V |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}$ | 1.51 | — |
| $\mathrm{Mn(OH)_3/Mn(OH)_2}$ | — | 0.13 |
| $\mathrm{O_2/H_2O}$ | 1.23 | 0.39 |
| $\mathrm{I_2/I^-}$ | 0.62 | 0.62 |
| $\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}/S_2O_3^{2-}}$ | 0.09 | 0.09 |

$$K_\mathrm{sp}(\mathrm{Mn(OH)_2})=1\times10^{-13},\qquad K_\mathrm{sp}(\mathrm{Mn(OH)_3})=1\times10^{-36}.$$

Gas constant: $R=8.315\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.statement:
To reduce volume variations, reagents are added either as solids (sodium hydroxide pellets, etc.) or as concentrated solutions (sulphuric acid).

1. The water to be tested is stored in a large container on the general-use bench. Place two glass beads in a $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ ground-top Erlenmeyer (conical) flask. Fill it to the rim with the water. The flask should stand in the basin provided to avoid overflow onto the bench. Measure the water temperature.
2. Add to the water, avoiding any loss of reagent: (a) $2\ \mathrm g$ of manganese(II) chloride, preweighed within a decigram and contained in the bag; (b) about eight sodium hydroxide pellets from the general-use bench, yielding a basic medium, pH $14$.
3. Stopper the flask, avoiding air bubbles, and swirl until the sodium hydroxide and manganese chloride have completely dissolved. A brown precipitate forms.
4. Let the flask stand for at least $30$ minutes.
5. Open the flask. Add concentrated sulphuric acid dropwise, stirring with a glass rod, until the solution is definitely acidic (check with pH indicator paper). Make sure that nearly all the precipitate has disappeared. Sulphuric acid is on the general-use bench.
6. Add $3\ \mathrm g$ of potassium iodide, preweighed within a decigram and contained in a bag. Stopper and shake until it dissolves. The solution should now be clear.
7. Remove a $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ sample and titrate it with an $X\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ sodium thiosulphate solution; the numerical value of $X$ will be shown on the board. The endpoint can be determined using thiodene, equivalent to starch. Dissolve a small quantity of this solid indicator in the solution just before the endpoint.

parts.statement: Justify that oxidation of manganese(II) by dissolved oxygen is possible only in alkaline solution.
Write the equations for the reactions between dissolved oxygen and manganese(II) hydroxide in alkaline solution; manganese(III) ions and iodide ions; and iodine and thiosulphate.
Record the volume of thiosulphate required to reach the endpoint.

Derive an expression relating the dissolved oxygen concentration in water, in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, to the volume in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of thiosulphate added at the endpoint. Determine this concentration for the tested water.

Deduce the volume of oxygen, in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ at $0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$ and a pressure of **101,325 Pa**, contained in a litre of water measured at ambient temperature. Give the water temperature.

sections.statement:
$$1\ \mathrm{mol\ O_2}\mathrel{\widehat=}4\ \mathrm{mol\ Mn(II)}\mathrel{\widehat=}4\ \mathrm{mol\ Mn(III)}$$

$$4\ \mathrm{mol\ Mn(III)}\mathrel{\widehat=}4\ \mathrm{mol\ I^-}\mathrel{\widehat=}2\ \mathrm{mol\ I_2}$$

$$2\ \mathrm{mol\ I_2}\mathrel{\widehat=}4\ \mathrm{mol\ S_2O_3^{2-}}$$

$$c(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}})\,V(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}})=4c(\mathrm{O_2})\times50.$$

problems.title: Problem 4 — Kinetics of an SN1 Reaction
problems.statement:
In aqueous ethanolic solution, tert-butyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylpropane) undergoes an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ nucleophilic substitution to form 2-methylpropan-2-ol and hydrochloric acid:

$$\text{tert-BuCl}+\mathrm{H_2O}=\text{tert-BuOH}+\mathrm{HCl}.$$

The rate law is:

$$\frac{d[\mathrm{HCl}]}{dt}=k_1[\text{tert-BuCl}].$$

The aim is to determine $k_1$ at ambient temperature.

sections.title: Procedure
sections.statement:
1. Pipette $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of tert-butyl chloride (flask 4.1 on the general-use bench) into a clean, dry $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ ground-neck Erlenmeyer (conical) flask.
2. As soon as possible, add $148\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the aqueous ethanol solution (flask 4.2 on the general-use bench), measured with a graduated cylinder.
3. Stopper the flask and stir vigorously with the magnetic stirrer. Start the timer. Carefully note the temperature $T(0)$ of the solution.
4. After approximately $5$, $15$, $25$, $35$, $45$ and $55$ minutes, determined accurately, pipette $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ samples into $20\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of an ice–acetone (propanone) mixture. Add two drops of bromothymol blue and titrate the liberated acid with $Y\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ aqueous sodium hydroxide; $Y$ will be shown on the board.

parts.statement:
The concentrations of tert-BuCl at $t=0$ and $t$ are related by:

$$\ln\frac{[\text{tert-BuCl}]_0}{[\text{tert-BuCl}]_t}=k_1t.$$

Establish:

$$\ln\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty-V}=k_1t,$$

where $V$ is the volume of sodium hydroxide used at time $t$ and $V(8)$ is its value at $t(8)$. The source defines:

$$t_\infty=t(8),\qquad V_\infty=V(8).$$
Calculate $V(8)$. Density of tert-BuCl at $20\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$: $850\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; molar mass: $92.5\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

Fill in the answer-sheet table with columns:

$$t\ (\mathrm{min}),\quad V\ (\mathrm{cm^3}),\quad V_\infty,\quad V,\quad\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty-V},\quad\ln\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty-V}.$$

Draw the curve:

$$\ln\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty-V}=f(t).$$

sections.statement:
$$\text{t-BuCl}+\mathrm{H_2O}\longrightarrow\text{t-BuOH}+\mathrm{HCl}.$$

| Time | t-BuCl | HCl formed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $t=0$ | $(\text{t-BuCl})_0$ | originally blank |
| $t$ | $(\text{t-BuCl})$ | $(\text{t-BuCl})_0-(\text{t-BuCl})$ |
| $t(8)$ | originally blank | $(\text{t-BuCl})_0$ |

The native derivative line is:

$$\frac{d(\mathrm{HCl})}{dt}=-\frac{(\text{t-BuCl})}{dt}=k_1(\text{t-BuCl}).$$

$$\ln\frac{(\text{t-BuCl})_0}{(\text{t-BuCl})}=k_1t.$$

At $t$:

$$c(\mathrm{HCl})=c_0(\text{t-BuCl})-c(\text{t-BuCl})=\frac{V(\mathrm{NaOH})c(\mathrm{NaOH})}{V(\mathrm{HCl})}=\frac{VY\times10^{-2}}{10}.$$

At $t(8)$:

$$c(\mathrm{HCl})=c_0(\text{t-BuCl})=\frac{aY}{10},\qquad c(\text{t-BuCl})=\frac{(a-V)Y}{10}.$$

$$\ln\frac{c_0(\text{t-BuCl})}{c(\text{t-BuCl})}=\ln\frac a{a-V}=k_1t.$$

solution.incompleteReason: The literal $t(8)$ and $V(8)$ notation, explicitly equated to infinity notation, is preserved. Question 4.4 asks for $t(0)$, while the procedure records $T(0)$. The key's derivative numerator lacks a $d$; its concentration line uses $VY10^{-2}/10$ before subsequent $aY/10$ expressions; the last expression uses numerator $170$, while $n_0$ uses $1.70$. These printed differences are retained. No board value $Y$, measured times, titres, temperature, completed answer table, graph, numerical rate constant or worked answers to 4.3–4.4 are supplied.
